summary: Defines a set of management objects for fault, configuration and performance management of applications from a system's viewpoint, in an SNMP management database. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines a standard set of counters and tables that a network management tool can read to see what software is installed on a machine and what is running there. The information comes from what the operating system already knows, so the applications themselves do not have to be modified to report anything.

subtitle: The SNMP objects that let a manager see which applications are installed and running on a host, without changing the applications.

tldr.problem: Managers need to know which applications are installed on a host, which of their files are present, and which processes are running, but most applications expose nothing about themselves and cannot be changed to do so.
tldr.mechanism: The System Application MIB defines tables for installed application packages and their elements, tables for running and past-run applications and processes, and a map table that works backwards from a process number to the application it belongs to, all filled in from information the host system already holds.
tldr.outcome: A management station can build a system-level view of the software on a host without any instrumentation inside the applications. The document also records the practical limits of the approach, including polling and the reuse of process numbers.

facts.label: Scalars controlling past run tables
facts.value: 2 per table: a maximum number of rows and a time limit

today: RFC 2287 is a Proposed Standard published in February 1998, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document itself says it does not specify a standard for the Internet community, and it asks that any later, more detailed application MIB refer back to this one.

sections.title: What This MIB Covers
sections.content:
This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. In particular, it describes a basic set of managed objects for fault, configuration and performance management of applications from a systems perspective. More specifically, the managed objects are restricted to information that can be determined from the system itself and which does not require special instrumentation within the applications to make the information available.

The memo notes that it does not specify a standard for the Internet community, in the sense of a protocol that implementations must interoperate on; it defines the names and meanings of the managed objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule that shapes the whole document is what information can be had for free. Anything that needs the application itself to cooperate is out of scope, because the applications being managed are usually third-party software.

sections.title: The SNMPv2 Framework It Builds On
sections.content:
The SNMPv2 Network Management Framework consists of the following major components: RFC 1902, Structure of Management Information for Version 2 of SNMP; RFC 1903, Textual Conventions for Version 2; RFC 1904, Conformance Statements for Version 2; RFC 1905, Protocol Operations for Version 2; RFC 1906, Transport Mappings for Version 2; RFC 1907, Management Information Base for Version 2; and RFC 1908, Coexistence between Version 1 and Version 2 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework. The framework permits new objects to be defined for the purpose of experimentation and evaluation.

Managed objects are accessed via a virtual information store, termed the Management Information Base. Objects in the MIB are defined using the subset of Abstract Syntax Notation One defined in the Structure of Management Information. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, an administratively assigned name. The object type together with an object instance serves to uniquely identify a specific instantiation of the object. For human convenience, a textual string, termed the object descriptor, is often used to refer to the object type.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is the catalog of named values that SNMP can read and write. Each entry has a number that identifies it on the network and a name that people use to talk about it.

sections.title: What an Application Is Here
sections.content:
The primary purpose of computing technologies is the execution of application software. These applications, typically specialized collections of executables, files and interprocess communications, exist to solve business, scientific or other problems. The configuration, fault detection, performance monitoring and control of application software across its life on a host computer is of great economic importance.

For the purposes of the work, the document defines applications as one or more units of executable code and other resources, installed on a single host system, that a manager may think of as a single object for management purposes.

The information described by the objects in the System Application MIB supports configuration, fault and performance management, and represents some of the basic attributes of application software from a systems, that is non-application-specific, perspective. The information allows for the description of applications as collections of executables and files installed and executing on a host computer.

The memo is concerned primarily with, and defines a model for, application information resident on a host computer which can be determined from the system itself and not from the individual applications. This system-level view of applications is designed to provide information about software applications installed and running on the host system without requiring modifications and code additions to the applications themselves. This approach was taken to insure ease and speed of implementation, while allowing room for future growth.
sections.plainLanguage: An application, for this MIB, is a package of programs and files installed on one machine, treated as one thing to manage. The goal is to describe it from the outside, the way the operating system sees it.

sections.title: How It Fits With Other MIBs
sections.content:
In the area of application management it is fully acknowledged and even expected that additional MIB modules will be defined over time to provide an even greater level of detail regarding applications. This MIB module presents the most general case: a set of management objects for providing generic information about applications whose object values can be determined from the computer system itself, without requiring instrumentation within the application.

A finer-grained level of detail is planned for the future appl MIB, which will be a common set of management objects relating to generic applications but which require some type of instrumentation in the application in order to be determined. Since the applmib MIB module will provide a finer level of detail, any connection to the sysAppl MIB should be made by having references from the more detailed appl MIB back to the more generic sysAppl MIB. Likewise, as application-specific MIB modules such as the WWW MIB are developed over time, these more specific MIBs should reference back to the more generic MIBs.

While this MIB module does not attempt to provide every detailed piece of information for managing applications, it does provide a basic systems-level view of the applications and their components on a single host system.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the coarse layer of a stack. A later MIB can describe applications in more detail, and the document asks that those detailed MIBs point back to this one rather than repeat it.

sections.title: The Groups and Tables
sections.content:
The System Application MIB structure models application packages as a whole, and also models the individual elements, the files and executables, which collectively form an application. The MIB is structured to model information regarding installed application packages and the elements which make up each application package. It also models activity information on applications, and in turn their components, that are running or have previously run on the host system. In modeling applications and their elements, the module provides the necessary link for associating executing processes with the applications of which they are a part.

The objects are arranged into three groups. The System Application Installed Group holds sysApplInstallPkgTable and sysApplInstallElmtTable; through these two tables administrators can determine which applications have been installed on a system and what their constituent components are. The first table lists the application packages installed on a particular host, and the second gives information about the executables and non-executable files which collectively compose an application. The MIB is intended to work with applications installed on a host, where installed means that the existence of the application and the association between an application and its component files can be discovered without additional instrumentation of the application itself. This may require conventions to be used, such as a central software installation mechanism or registry; many UNIX systems use a utility such as pkgadd to track installed application packages, while many PC systems use a global registry.

The System Application Run Group holds sysApplRunTable, sysApplPastRunTable, sysApplElmtRunTable and sysApplElmtPastRunTable, together with scalars for restricting table sizes. The System Application Map Group holds the single sysApplMapTable.

For each category the MIB first treats an application package as a whole, and then breaks down the package to provide information about each of its elements.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three groups of tables. One says what is installed and what files make it up. One says what is running now and what ran before. The last one works backwards, from a running process to the package it came from.

sections.title: What the Run Tables Record
sections.content:
The sysApplRunTable contains the application instances currently running on the host. Each time an application is invoked, a new entry is created to provide information about that particular invocation, and the entry remains until the application instance terminates, at which time it is deleted from the run table and placed in the sysApplPastRunTable. The past run table maintains a history of instances of applications which have previously executed on the host.

Because the past run table will continuously grow as applications are executed and terminate, two scalars control the aging-out of entries: sysApplPastRunMaxRows specifies the maximum number of entries the table may contain, and sysApplPastRunTblTimeLimit specifies the maximum age of the table entries. The oldest entries are removed first. The two tables contain entries for each invocation of an application: a single application package might be invoked multiple times, and each invocation is recorded by a separate entry.

To implement this group, the agent must be able to recognize that an application has been invoked and to determine when that invocation terminates. This poses a complex problem, since a single application invocation may involve numerous processes, some of which may be required to remain running throughout the duration of the application and others which might come and go. The sysApplInstallElmtRole columnar object is meant to assist in this task, by indicating which element is the application's primary executable, which elements must be running for the application to be running, and which elements are dependent on required elements.

The sysApplElmtRunTable contains an entry for every process currently running on the host, so that the information on the load on the system is complete. However, when processes terminate, only information from entries corresponding to elements of an identified application is moved to the sysApplElmtPastRunTable. If a process cannot be associated with any parent application, it is simply removed from the run table, which allows processes such as ps or grep to show up in the run table, where they are consuming resources and are thus interesting, but not in the past run table.

The map group's single table provides a backwards mapping: given a known process identification number, the corresponding invoked application, installed element and installed application package can be quickly determined. The table contains one entry for each process currently executing on the system, and a management application is expected to use it by doing a GetNext operation with the known process ID number as the partial instance identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Each time a program starts, the agent is supposed to notice and make a note. When it stops, the note moves to a history table that is trimmed by age and by size. A process that belongs to no known application is still listed as running, because it is using resources, but it does not enter the history.

sections.title: Implementation Issues
sections.content:
Implementations of the System Application MIB on popular operating systems might require some considerable processing power to obtain status information from the managed resources, and it might be difficult to determine when an application or a process starts or finishes. Implementors might therefore choose an implementation approach where the agent polls the managed resources at regular intervals. The information retrieved by every poll is used to update a cached version of this MIB maintained inside the agent, and SNMP requests are processed based on the information found in that cache.

A scalar sysApplAgentPollInterval gives the manager control over the polling frequency. There is a trade-off between the amount of resources consumed during every poll to update the cache and the accuracy of the information provided by the agent. A default value of 60 seconds is defined to keep the processing overhead low while providing usable information for long-lived processes. A manager is expected to adjust this value if more accurate information about short-lived applications or processes is needed, or if the resources consumed by the agent are too high.

The document also records a corner case in the past run table for elements. It is indexed by the tuple of the application invocation identifier and the process identifier, because many systems re-use process ID numbers that are no longer assigned to running processes; typically, the process numbers wrap and the next available number is used. A collision is therefore still possible, though unlikely: an element of an invocation runs and terminates and moves to the past run table, the process numbering numbers wrap, the same invocation has another element run and is assigned the same process number as the earlier one, and that element terminates and moves to the past run table before the older duplicate entry has been aged out. In the event that a collision occurs, the new entry will replace the old entry.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling the operating system when a program starts and stops takes work, so an agent may instead look at the machine every minute and keep its own copy of the answer. The document also warns that process numbers get reused, so the history of past processes can occasionally contain a duplicate that overwrites an earlier one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
In order to implement this MIB, an agent must make certain management information available about various logical and physical entities within a managed system, which may be considered sensitive in some network environments.

Therefore, a network administrator may wish to employ instance-level access control, and configure the access mechanism, that is the community strings in SNMPv1 and SNMPv2C, such that certain instances within this MIB are excluded from particular MIB views.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB exposes what software a machine runs and where its files are, which may be sensitive information. Access to individual entries can therefore be restricted rather than exposing the whole table.

viz.caption: THE GROUPS AND TABLES OF THE SYSTEM APPLICATION MIB
THE ROLE BITS OF AN INSTALLED ELEMENT

items.title: executable
items.text: The element is an executable; the other bits mean nothing if it is not.

items.title: exclusive
items.text: Only one copy of this element may run per invocation.

items.title: primary
items.text: The application's one primary executable; running it is what counts as an invocation.

items.title: required
items.text: All required elements must be running for the application to count as running and healthy.

items.title: dependent
items.text: Dependent elements may not run unless the required ones do.

items.title: unknown
items.text: The default when an operator cannot say what the element's role is.

viz.caption: THE RUN STATE VALUES REPORTED FOR A PROCESS

items.label: running
items.desc: The current execution state of a running application or process.

items.label: runnable
items.desc: Waiting for a resource such as CPU.

viz.caption: THE TWO PRACTICAL ISSUES THE DOCUMENT FLAGS

items.title: Polling the host
items.text: The agent may read the system at intervals and answer from a cache.

items.title: Polling interval
items.text: sysApplAgentPollInterval, 60 seconds by default, set by the manager.

items.title: Why it is a trade-off
items.text: Shorter intervals give more accurate data for short-lived processes and cost more resources.

items.title: Reused process numbers
items.text: Many systems wrap and reuse process ID numbers, so the past run table can hold duplicates.

items.title: How a duplicate is handled
items.text: The newer entry replaces the older one in the past run table.
